newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigeria sends more troops into Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria sends more troops into Sierra Leone.

text.p: Nigeria sent more troops to Sierra Leone on Wednesday and Ghana sent negotiators, both hoping to persuade leaders of a 10-day-old coup to back down.
Freetown residents streamed out to the provinces, taking no chances after Monday's fighting between Nigerian troops, Sierra Leonean coup soldiers and their rebel allies.
Two French navy frigates evacuated 734 foreign nationals, many of them from French-speaking West African countries.

Ghana's deputy foreign minister, Victor Gbeho, and Brigadier Seth Obeng, chief of staff at army headquarters, left Monrovia for Freetown after talks with commanders of the Nigeria-led ECOMOG force, which has troops in Sierra Leone.

Scores of ECOMOG troops flew to Freetown by helicopter to keep up pressure on leaders of the May 25 coup, which turned bloody on Monday after Nigerian gunboats shelled the city and dissident soldiers and rebel allies turned on Nigerian soldiers.
Residents have virtually abandoned the seafront Aberdeen district, which was hit by shells on Monday, fleeing either into the city centre or to the interior.
Liberian refugees fled the Jui camp, which lies between the Nigerian base and positions of Sierra Leonean troops and rebels of the Revolutionary United Front.

Refugee spokesman Mac Varney Rogers said the camp's 5,000 population had moved to a disused airfield nearby where they were no longer in the line of fire but were sleeping in the open air. "When it rains, we get soaked," he said.
A spokesman for the coup leaders said they had freed 300 Nigerian soldiers whom they captured on Monday to hold as human shields against air raids.
ECOMOG, which did not comment on the reports until the Nigerians' release was announced, said none of its men were held hostage.
U.N. sources said some Nigerians had been detained when they went to rescue troops from a hotel at the centre of the fighting on Monday, but the number of 300 seemed rather high.
"All of our soldiers are accounted for in the two locations we occupied in Freetown," said ECOMOG Field Commander General Victor Malu.

All over town, families stood with bundles of belongings waiting for communal taxis to take them to truck parks on the edge of Freetown where they hoped to find a ride to the interior. Rebels roved around the city in looted vehicles.

"If use of force becomes a last resort and is inevitable, it may have to come to that," U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters during a stopover in London, adding that the coup leaders lacked support at home and abroad.
Sierra Leone, a former British colony racked by civil war since 1991, has suffered three coups in five years. It is one of the world's poorest countries despite a wealth of minerals.
The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit called for the restoration of ousted civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who is in neighbouring Guinea.

"We unanimously and unreservedly condemned the coup d'etat in Sierra Leone as an enormous setback for democracy in Africa," Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe, the new OAU chairman, told the closing session of the summit in his capital Harare.
Coup leaders put the death toll in Monday's bombardment and fighting at 80. Other sources accused the military of exaggerating and said it was no more than 50.

The United States carried out its largest single-day non-combatant evacuation from the city on Tuesday, bringing out 1,261 civilians by helicopter to Guinea. Britain chartered a Boeing 747 to bring evacuees from Guinea to London on Thursday.
The coup leaders accused Kabbah of failing to consolidate a peace accord signed last November with rebel leader Foday Sankoh, and of encouraging ethnic conflict.
Sankoh, named vice-chairman in Major Johnny Paul Koromah's ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council, is being held in Nigeria. He has told his men to back the coup.
